## <span class="num">11.2.1</span> Actions of a Group on Itself

A group acts on itself in two basic ways. Under left multiplication, $g \cdot h = gh$, the action is transitive, every stabilizer is trivial, and no $g \neq e$ has a fixed point. In particular the action is faithful, which gives Cayley’s theorem (Theorem [3.2.14](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#theorem-3-2-14)): a finite group $G$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_n$, where $n = |G|$. This embedding tells us little about the structure of $G$. The second action is far more informative.

The group $G$ also acts on itself by conjugation, $g \cdot h = ghg^{-1}$. Each map $h \mapsto ghg^{-1}$ is an automorphism of $G$, and $g \mapsto (h \mapsto ghg^{-1})$ is a homomorphism $G \to \Aut(G) \subseteq \Sym(G)$, so this is indeed an action. Recall from Definition [3.2.12](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#definition-3-2-12) that its orbits are the conjugacy classes $C_h = \{ghg^{-1} : g \in G\}$, and that the stabilizer of $h$ is its *centralizer* $Z(h) = \{g \in G : gh = hg\}$, the subgroup of elements that commute with $h$; we write $Z_G(h)$ when the group must be named. The kernel of the action is the center $Z(G) = \bigcap_{h \in G} Z(h)$ (Definition [3.1.13](/notes/math-55a/3-1-cosets-and-quotient-groups#definition-3-1-13)).

:::note
The conjugation action is trivial (every element is fixed) if and only if $G$ is abelian, and it is faithful if and only if $Z(G) = \{e\}$. A subgroup $N \leq G$ is normal if and only if it is a union of conjugacy classes (Proposition [3.2.13](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-13)); it contains the class $\{e\}$, and by Lagrange’s theorem its order divides $|G|$. We use this repeatedly to find normal subgroups.
:::

## <span class="num">11.2.2</span> The Class Equation

By Proposition [3.2.13](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-13), the conjugacy class of $h$ has $|C_h| = [G : Z(h)]$ elements, a divisor of $|G|$ when $G$ is finite, and $|C_h| = 1$ if and only if $h \in Z(G)$.

:::theorem{11.2.1} The Class Equation
Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $h_1, \ldots, h_r$ be representatives of the conjugacy classes of $G$ with more than one element. Then $$|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^{r} [G : Z(h_i)],$$ where each $[G : Z(h_i)] = |C_{h_i}|$ divides $|G|$ and is greater than 1.
:::

:::proof
The conjugacy classes partition $G$. The classes with one element are the sets $\{z\}$ with $z \in Z(G)$, and together they contain $|Z(G)|$ elements. The other classes are $C_{h_1}, \ldots, C_{h_r}$, and $|C_{h_i}| = [G : Z(h_i)]$ by the Orbit–Stabilizer Theorem.
:::

:::example{11.2.2} The class equation of $S_3$
By Theorem [3.4.6](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-6), the conjugacy classes of $S_3$ are $\{e\}$, the three transpositions, and the two 3-cycles. So $Z(S_3) = \{e\}$ and the class equation is $6 = 1 + 3 + 2$. We compute more class equations in Section [11.4](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n).
:::

## <span class="num">11.2.3</span> $p$-Groups

:::definition{11.2.3} $p$-group
Let $p$ be a prime. A finite group $G$ is a ***$p$-group*** if $|G| = p^k$ for some $k \geq 0$.
:::

:::theorem{11.2.4} $p$-groups have nontrivial center
If $G$ is a $p$-group and $G \neq \{e\}$, then $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$. In particular $|Z(G)| \geq p$.
:::

:::proof
Let $|G| = p^k$ with $k \geq 1$. In the class equation each $[G : Z(h_i)]$ divides $p^k$ and is greater than 1, so it is divisible by $p$. Hence $|Z(G)| = |G| - \sum_i [G : Z(h_i)]$ is divisible by $p$. Since $e \in Z(G)$, $|Z(G)| \geq 1$, and therefore $|Z(G)| \geq p$.
:::

:::corollary{11.2.5} Groups of order $p^2$
If $|G| = p^2$ with $p$ prime, then $G$ is abelian, and $G \cong \ZZ/p^2$ or $G \cong \ZZ/p \times \ZZ/p$.
:::

:::proof
By Theorem [11.2.4](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#theorem-11-2-4), $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$, and $|Z(G)|$ divides $p^2$ by Lagrange’s theorem, so $|Z(G)|$ is $p$ or $p^2$. Suppose $|Z(G)| = p$, and pick $g \notin Z(G)$. The centralizer $Z(g)$ contains $Z(G)$ and $g$, so $|Z(g)| > p$; as a subgroup of $G$ its order divides $p^2$, so $Z(g) = G$. Then $g$ commutes with every element, so $g \in Z(G)$, a contradiction. Hence $Z(G) = G$ and $G$ is abelian. By the classification of finitely generated abelian groups (Theorem [10.2.1](/notes/math-55a/10-2-classification-of-finitely-generated-abelian-groups#theorem-10-2-1)), $G$ is a product of cyclic groups whose orders multiply to $p^2$, so $G \cong \ZZ/p^2$ or $G \cong \ZZ/p \times \ZZ/p$. These are not isomorphic, since only the first has an element of order $p^2$.
:::

The next lemma is elementary, and we use it several times in this chapter.

:::lemma{11.2.6} Subgroups of index 2
Let $H$ be a subgroup of index 2 in a group $G$. Then $H$ is normal in $G$, and $g^2 \in H$ for every $g \in G$. In particular, $H$ contains every element of $G$ of odd order.
:::

:::proof
The subgroup $H$ is normal by Proposition [3.1.11](/notes/math-55a/3-1-cosets-and-quotient-groups#proposition-3-1-11). The quotient $G/H$ has order 2, so $(gH)^2 = H$, that is, $g^2 \in H$. If $g$ has odd order $2k + 1$, then $g = g^{2k+2} = (g^{k+1})^2 \in H$.
:::

:::proposition{11.2.7} Groups of order 8
Up to isomorphism there are exactly five groups of order 8: the abelian groups $\ZZ/8$, $\ZZ/4 \times \ZZ/2$ and $(\ZZ/2)^3$, the dihedral group $D_4$ of symmetries of the square, and the ***quaternion group*** $Q_8 = \{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$, in which $-1$ commutes with every element, $(-1)^2 = 1$, multiplication by $-1$ changes signs, and $$i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = -1, \qquad ij = -ji = k, \qquad jk = -kj = i, \qquad ki = -ik = j.$$
:::

:::proof
First, $Q_8$ is a group. In $\GL_2(\CC)$, the matrices $A = \begin{psmallmatrix} i & 0 \\ 0 & -i \end{psmallmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ satisfy $A^2 = B^2 = (AB)^2 = -I$, $BA = -AB$, $B(AB) = A$ and $(AB)A = B$. So the eight distinct matrices $\pm I, \pm A, \pm B, \pm AB$ multiply by the rules above, with $1, i, j, k$ replaced by $I, A, B, AB$; they form a subgroup of $\GL_2(\CC)$, and $Q_8$ is a group isomorphic to it.

The three abelian groups listed are pairwise non-isomorphic (the largest orders of their elements are 8, 4 and 2), and by Theorem [10.2.1](/notes/math-55a/10-2-classification-of-finitely-generated-abelian-groups#theorem-10-2-1) every abelian group of order 8 is one of them. The groups $D_4$ and $Q_8$ are not abelian, and they are not isomorphic: $D_4$ has five elements of order 2 (the four reflections and the rotation by $\pi$), while $-1$ is the only element of order 2 in $Q_8$.

Now let $G$ be a non-abelian group of order 8. No element of $G$ has order 8, since $G$ is not cyclic. If every element satisfied $g^2 = e$, then $ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1} = ba$ for all $a, b$, and $G$ would be abelian. So some $a \in G$ has order 4. The subgroup $N = \langle a \rangle$ has index 2, so it is normal by Lemma [11.2.6](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#lemma-11-2-6). Fix $b \notin N$. Then $G = N \sqcup Nb$, and every element of $G$ can be written uniquely as $a^i b^k$ with $0 \leq i \leq 3$ and $k \in \{0, 1\}$.

Since $N$ is normal, $bab^{-1} \in N$, and it has order 4, so $bab^{-1} \in \{a, a^3\}$. If $bab^{-1} = a$, then $a$ and $b$ commute and $G$, whose elements are the $a^i b^k$, is abelian. Hence $bab^{-1} = a^{-1}$, and so $b a^j = a^{-j} b$ for all $j$. By Lemma [11.2.6](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#lemma-11-2-6), $b^2 \in N$, say $b^2 = a^j$; since $b$ commutes with $b^2$, we get $a^j = b a^j b^{-1} = a^{-j}$, so $a^{2j} = e$ and $b^2 \in \{e, a^2\}$. Now $$(a^i b^k)(a^j b^l) = a^{i + (-1)^k j}\, b^k b^l, \qquad b^k b^l \in \{e, b, b^2\},$$ so the multiplication of $G$ is completely determined by whether $b^2 = e$ or $b^2 = a^2$.

- If $b^2 = e$, the same rules hold in $D_4$ for $a$ the rotation by $\pi/2$ and $b$ a reflection, whose products $a^i b^k$ are the eight elements of $D_4$. So $a^i b^k \mapsto a^i b^k$ is an isomorphism $G \cong D_4$.
- If $b^2 = a^2$, the same rules hold in $Q_8$ for $a = i$ and $b = j$: $i$ has order 4, $j^2 = -1 = i^2$, and $jij^{-1} = ji(-j) = -(ji)j = kj = -i = i^{-1}$. The elements $i^m j^l$ are $1, i, -1, -i, j, k, -j, -k$, so $G \cong Q_8$.
:::

:::note
The class equation gives another way into this classification. If $G$ is non-abelian of order 8, then $|Z(G)| \in \{2, 4\}$ by Theorem [11.2.4](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#theorem-11-2-4), and the argument of Corollary [11.2.5](/notes/math-55a/11-2-conjugation-and-the-class-equation#corollary-11-2-5) rules out 4: for $g \notin Z(G)$, $Z(g)$ contains $Z(G)$ and $g$, so it would have more than 4 elements and be all of $G$. So $|Z(G)| = 2$. For each $g \notin Z(G)$, the centralizer $Z(g)$ lies strictly between $Z(G)$ and $G$, so it has order 4 and $|C_g| = 2$. The class equation is therefore $8 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2$: two central elements and three classes of size 2. One can then work out the possible multiplications from there.
:::
